claims.text: Optimized SPS using nano-sized ZrB2 powder can produce fully densified, single-phase ZrB2 at 1900–2000 °C.
The starting material should be high-reactivity, nano-sized ZrB2 powder with a narrow, homogeneous particle-size distribution.
The SPS process should use a heating rate of about 100 °C/min, a peak temperature of 1900–2000 °C, a dwell time initially set to 5–10 minutes, and 50–100 MPa uniaxial pressure.
The SPS process should be conducted under a reducing atmosphere to prevent oxidation.
Optimizing dwell time and pressure can reduce residual-stress development while retaining complete densification.
SPS at 1900–2000 °C represents a lower preparation temperature than conventional ZrB2 sintering above 2300 °C.
The intervention will create a dense microstructure with minimal porosity, uniform grain boundaries, and reduced residual stress.
SPS combines localized Joule heating and applied pressure to enhance atomic diffusion and particle rearrangement.
Enhanced diffusion and particle rearrangement enable ZrB2 densification at lower temperature.
Optimizing SPS time and pressure minimizes residual stresses that could cause nonuniform grain growth or defects.
Residual pores and other defects act as sites that accelerate corrosion during liquid-plating exposure.
Optimized SPS-processed ZrB2 will have fewer residual pores and a more uniform microstructure than conventionally sintered ZrB2 prepared near or above 2300 °C.
The optimized SPS material will have greater mechanical strength than conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2.
The optimized SPS material will better resist prolonged liquid-plating corrosion and consequently form fewer holes and experience fewer component failures.
Conventionally sintered ZrB2 prepared above 2300 °C typically has higher porosity and more microstructural defects that cause failure during long-term liquid-plating exposure.
The preparation boundary is SPS at 1900–2000 °C, and the service boundary is long-duration exposure to a liquid-plating bath.
SPS specimens with varied dwell times and pressures should be compared against a conventionally sintered control prepared above 2300 °C.
Density, porosity, grain boundaries, phase purity, residual stress, mechanical strength, weight loss, and hole formation can be measured to test the hypothesis.

The hypothesis is falsified if SPS specimens show no statistically significant reduction in porosity or improvement in strength, corrosion resistance, and hole formation relative to the conventional control.
